MEMORANDUM

TO: Engagement Team — Arbitration International Dispute Resolution
FROM: Counsel
RE: Analysis of Counterparty Markup of the Arbitration Agreement — Accept/Reject/Counter Recommendations
DATE: [Matter Date]
MATTER: arbitration-international-dispute-resolution — Analyze Counterparty Markup of Arbitration Agreement and Prepare Accept/Reject/Counter Memorandum

I. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

We have reviewed the counterparty's latest redline markup of the arbitration agreement (the "Agreement") against (i) our original draft, (ii) the relevant excerpts of the underlying stock/asset purchase agreement (the "SPA"), and (iii) our internal playbook on international dispute-resolution provisions. The counterparty's markup introduces a series of deviations, several of which are material and, if accepted, would meaningfully shift the procedural and cost economics of any future dispute resolution in the counterparty's favor, while also creating enforceability and scope risks inconsistent with our form and market practice.

In summary, we recommend: (1) ACCEPT two administrative/clarifying changes that align with market standard; (2) REJECT or COUNTER the four material deviations concerning AAA vs. ICC administration, seat selection (New York vs. a permissive/alternative seat), consolidation and joinder, and arbitrator number/qualifications; and (3) REJECT the carve-outs that would whittle down the scope of disputes subject to arbitration. Our detailed recommendation for each redline item follows, grounded in the original draft, the SPA, and the internal playbook.

II. MATERIALS REVIEWED

1. Original Draft of the Arbitration Agreement (the version negotiated and circulated as the baseline).
2. Counterparty Redline/Markup (the counterparty's proposed tracked changes to the original draft).
3. SPA Excerpts (the operative purchase agreement containing the repurchase/dispute-residual interplay relevant to the arbitration clause's scope).
4. Internal Playbook — Arbitration International Dispute Resolution (firm precedent on seat, institutional rules, arbitrator panels, consolidation/joinder, and scope drafting).

Each deviation is analyzed below against these four reference points.

III. REDLINE-BY-REDLINE ANALYSIS AND RECOMMENDATIONS

A. Institutional Rules — Adoption of AAA Rules for an International Dispute (MARKUP — Material)

Original Draft: Provided for arbitration administered by the International Chamber of Commerce (ICC) under the ICC Rules, with the ICC International Court of Arbitration serving as appointing authority, consistent with our playbook's preference for international administration of cross-border disputes.

Counterparty Markup: Replaces ICC administration with the American Arbitration Association (AAA) and the Commercial Arbitration Rules (and Mediation Procedures).

Analysis: Our playbook directs that for international disputes involving parties in more than one seat, institutional administration should be international (ICC, or LCIA/SIAC as appropriate) to ensure neutrality, standardized international procedure (including the emergency-arbitrator provisions and expedited thresholds under the ICC Rules), and a tribunal appointment process understood by counterpart foreign courts. The counterparty's proposal to administer under AAA Commercial Rules is an international-vs.-domestic procedural mismatch; the AAA Commercial Rules are optimized for domestic U.S. arbitration and do not carry the same international appointing-authority safeguards or award-recognition conventions support that the ICC's framework does. Acceptance would erode neutrality and complicate any enforcement where the counterparty or its assets sit outside the U.S. We also note the change would alter the default arbitrator-selection and challenge procedures.

Recommended Position: REJECT / COUNTER. Hold the ICC administration coupled with a recognized international appointing authority. As a fallback counter, we could accept AAA administration ONLY if (i) the International Centre for Dispute Resolution (ICDR) International Arbitration Rules are substituted for the Commercial Rules and (ii) the seat remains as set forth below.

B. Seat of Arbitration (MARKUP — Material)

Original Draft: Seat of arbitration in New York, New York, United States, with the procedural law of the seat governing the arbitration, consistent with the SPA's governing-law and forum selection for the underlying transaction.

Counterparty Markup: Changes the seat to a party-neutral/permissive formulation, and/or relocates the seat to the counterparty's home jurisdiction (or a location inconvenient to the client), while retaining New York governing law for the contract generally.

Analysis: Seat selection determines curial law, the available supervisory courts, and, critically, where any award can most readily be challenged. The counterparty's proposed seat (a) is inconsistent with the SPA's New York forum and choice-of-law scheme, creating a mismatch between the transactional and the dispute-resolution regimes, and (b) shifts the venue cost and enforcement burden against our client. Under our playbook, the seat should be stable, arbitration-friendly, and consistent with the governing transaction documents; we do not deviate absent compelling, reciprocal commercial reason.

Recommended Position: REJECT. Maintain the New York seat, matching the SPA. If the counterparty seeks flexibility, offer a counter limited to a defined alternative-seat menu (e.g., New York or London, at claimant's option) without prejudice to the client, rather than a unilateral relocation.

C. Scope of Disputes Subject to Arbitration (MARKUP — Material)

Original Draft: Arbitration covers "all disputes, controversies, or claims arising out of or relating to this Agreement, including any question regarding its existence, validity, or termination," mirroring the broad arbitration-scope language in our playbook and aligned with the SPA's indemnification and repurchase provisions.

Counterparty Markup: Adds carve-outs excluding (i) equitable/injunctive relief actions, (ii) actions to enforce confidentiality and non-solicitation covenants, and (iii) claims for specific performance of the closing conditions, from arbitration and reserving them to court.

Analysis: These carve-outs are designed to allow the counterparty to litigate its most valuable remedies in court while compelling the client into arbitration for claims the counterparty prefers to slow down. Under our playbook, carve-outs of this kind are disfavored unless the underlying SPA affirmatively preserves such court-based forums. Here the SPA does not reserve these remedies to a court; introducing them in the arbitration agreement unilaterally expands scope and creates forum-splitting risk (parallel proceedings, inconsistent results, and duplicative cost). Broad, one-stop arbitration preserves efficiency and avoids the very fragmentation the carve-outs invite.

Recommended Position: REJECT the new carve-outs. Hold the "arising out of or relating to" all-claims formulation. If the counterparty insists on an equitable-relief carve-out, counter with the narrower and standard-market formulation limiting any such carve-out to preliminary injunctive relief "in aid of and pending" arbitration under the ICC Rules / supervisory court, preserving the arbitral forum as the forum for the merits.

D. Consolidation, Joinder, and Multi-Party Provisions (MARKUP — Material)

Original Draft: Permits consolidation with related disputes and joinder of affiliates, in line with our playbook's recommendation for integrated dispute resolution across related agreements in the deal structure.

Counterparty Markup: Strikes or restricts consolidation/joinder rights, confining arbitration to the two signatories and prohibiting consolidation with disputes arising under related transaction documents (including the SPA and ancillary agreements).

Analysis: The underlying transaction is integrated — the SPA and the arbitration agreement operate as a single dispute-resolution scheme. Eliminating consolidation/joinder rights would force related disputes to proceed in parallel in different forums, increasing cost, creating irreconcilable-results risk, and undermining the one-stop-economics the client negotiated. This is a net negative for the client's position and inconsistent with our playbook.

Recommended Position: REJECT / COUNTER. Restore consolidation and joinder rights permitting the client to consolidate related disputes arising under the same or related transaction documents. As a counter, we can narrow to consolidation at the tribunal's discretion upon motion, rather than as-of-right, to reduce the counterparty's objection surface.

E. Number and Qualifications of Arbitrators (MARKUP — Material)

Original Draft: A three-member tribunal, with each party appointing one arbitrator and the two party-appointed arbitrators appointing the chair, with no nationality restrictions, consistent with the international character of the matter and our playbook's default.

Counterparty Markup: Changes the panel to a sole arbitrator (or otherwise restricts the chair's nationality / adds a requirement that all arbitrators hold a specific bar or reside in a specified jurisdiction).

Analysis: For a dispute arising from an international transaction, a single arbitrator of a specified nationality/bar unfairly narrows the candidate pool and removes the balance and specialized expertise of a three-member panel, particularly on complex valuation/indemnification issues that surface under the SPA. Restricting nationality or bar membership is also an enforceability and neutrality concern under international standards. Our playbook retains a three-member panel with neutral chair selection for international matters.

Recommended Position: REJECT / COUNTER. Maintain the three-member tribunal with party-appointed members and a chair appointed by the two party-appointed arbitrators. As a modest counter-accommodation, we can agree that the chair shall not share the nationality of any party (a common neutrality safeguard), but reject the counterparty's sole-arbitrator or bar-restriction proposal.

F. Administrative / Non-Substantive Markups (ACCEPT)

The counterparty's markup also contains minor administrative and stylistic changes (e.g., notice-provider designation, typographical corrections, definitional cross-references, and clarification of the award-delivery mechanism). These are consistent with market practice, do not alter substantive rights, and align with our internal playbook's formatting preference. We recommend ACCEPT these items without comment, subject to conforming changes so they remain consistent with the retained substantive positions in Sections III.A–E above.

IV. SPA CONSISTENCY REVIEW

We have reconciled each of the counterparty's material deviations against the SPA excerpts. The SPA: (i) selects New York law and forum; (ii) contemplates integrated dispute resolution across the transaction documents; and (iii) contains no reservation of equitable relief, specific performance, or confidentiality remedies to a separate court forum. Consequently, the majority of the counterparty's markup is not merely a deviation from our form but is affirmatively inconsistent with the SPA's own dispute-resolution scheme. Where a conflict arises between the arbitration agreement and the SPA, the parties' stated intent that they operate as a single scheme weighs in favor of accepting only those markups consistent with the SPA (i.e., the administrative items) and rejecting those that fragment the scheme (the seat change, scope carve-outs, and consolidation elimination).

V. RECOMMENDATIONS SUMMARY

| # | Provision | Counterparty Position | Recommendation |
|---|-----------|----------------------|----------------|
| A | Institutional Rules | AAA Commercial (vs. ICC international) | REJECT / COUNTER — hold ICC; fallback to ICDR International |
| B | Seat of Arbitration | Unilateral/mismatched seat | REJECT — hold New York seat per SPA |
| C | Scope Carve-Outs | Exclude equity/specific performance/confidentiality | REJECT — hold all-claims; narrow counter only for injunctive relief in aid of arbitration |
| D | Consolidation/Joinder | Restrict to signatories / bar consolidation | REJECT / COUNTER — restore consolidation; discretionary counter available |
| E | Arbitrator Panel | Sole arbitrator / nationality-bar restriction | REJECT / COUNTER — hold 3-member panel; neutral-chair nationality counter |
| F | Administrative Items | Clarifying/style changes | ACCEPT |

VI. NEXT STEPS

Upon approval of the recommended positions, we will: (1) circulate a conformed counter-redline incorporating Sections III.A–E and the Section III.F acceptances; (2) flag the three highest-priority items (seat, institutional rules, scope carve-outs) for the negotiation call with counterparty counsel; and (3) confirm the SPA-conformity position with the deal team before circulating. We recommend sequencing the material items first to lock in the framework before the administrative acceptances.

This memorandum is privileged and confidential, prepared in connection with the requested arbitration international dispute resolution analysis, and reflects our recommendations based on the materials reviewed as of the date of this memo.
